name: Incessant Rain
description: Note the unusual memory limit. Silver Wolf gives you an array $$$a$$$ of length $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ queries. In each query, she replaces an element in $$$a$$$. After each query, she asks you to output the maximum integer $$$k$$$ such that there exists an integer $$$x$$$ such that it is the $$$k$$$-majority of a subarray$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ of $$$a$$$. An integer $$$y$$$ is the $$$k$$$-majority of array $$$b$$$ if $$$y$$$ appears at least $$$\lfloor \frac{|b|+1}{2} \rfloor +k$$$ times in $$$b$$$, where $$$|b|$$$ represents the length of $$$b$$$. Note that $$$b$$$ may not necessarily have a $$$k$$$-majority. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$An array $$$b$$$ is a subarray of an array $$$a$$$ if $$$b$$$ can be obtained from $$$a$$$ by the deletion of several (possibly, zero or all) elements from the beginning and several (possibly, zero or all) elements from the end.
input_specification: The first line contains an integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^4$$$)  — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \leq n, q \leq 3 \cdot 10^5$$$)  — the length of $$$a$$$ and the number of queries. The following line contains $$$n$$$ space-separated integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq a_i \leq n$$$). The following $$$q$$$ lines contain two integers $$$i$$$ and $$$x$$$, denoting the query that replaces $$$a_i$$$ with $$$x$$$ ($$$1 \leq i, x \leq n$$$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ and the sum of $$$q$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$3 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output the answer to all queries on a single new line, separated by a space.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2117H — Incessant Rain [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
